genZNote: It takes fewer than 20 viral particles to infect you — which is exactly why one sick person can take down an entire cruise ship.

habitat.hostAssociation: Infects intestinal epithelial cells; humans are the primary reservoir
habitat.reservoir: Infected humans, including those shedding virus for weeks after symptoms resolve

identificationClues: Diagnosed by RT-PCR of stool (the standard method, since the virus is difficult to culture routinely)
Extremely low infectious dose (as few as 10-20 viral particles) and prolonged environmental persistence drive rapid outbreaks
Classic setting: cruise ships, nursing homes, schools, and other closed/crowded communal settings
Acute onset of vomiting and watery, non-bloody diarrhea, usually resolving within 24-72 hours

diseases: Acute viral gastroenteritis — sudden-onset vomiting, watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and low-grade fever, typically self-limited
clinicalImportance.transmission: Fecal-oral route, including person-to-person contact, contaminated food/water, and contaminated surfaces/fomites; can also aerosolize during vomiting
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: The leading cause of acute gastroenteritis outbreaks worldwide across all age groups, notoriously associated with cruise ships, healthcare facilities, and schools due to its very low infectious dose and environmental hardiness
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: RT-PCR of stool is the standard diagnostic method; alcohol-based hand sanitizers are less effective against norovirus than soap-and-water handwashing, an important infection-control point

examFacts.keyBiochemicalReaction: Not applicable — diagnosed by RT-PCR of stool
examFacts.importantDisease: Acute viral gastroenteritis — leading cause worldwide
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: A non-enveloped virus with an extremely low infectious dose, making it the classic cause of explosive outbreaks in cruise ships, schools, and healthcare facilities
